reference.source: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Now understood as greater trochanteric pain syndrome, in which gluteal tendinopathy rather than primary bursal inflammation is the usual driver
Presents with lateral hip pain aggravated by lying on the affected side, prolonged standing, stairs and single-leg loading
Tenderness is localised over the greater trochanter
More common in women and in middle to older age
Provocative tests include resisted hip abduction and prolonged single-leg stance
Ultrasound or MRI can show gluteus medius and minimus tendinopathy with secondary bursal change
Management centres on load modification, restoring hip abductor function with physiotherapy and avoiding provocative positions rather than rest alone
Corticosteroid injection may give short-term relief but does not address the underlying tendon problem and carries a recurrence risk
reference.pathophysiology: Lateral hip pain historically attributed to inflammation of the trochanteric bursae is now recognised in most cases as greater trochanteric pain syndrome, driven by degenerative tendinopathy of the gluteus medius and minimus tendons at their insertion on the greater trochanter, often with secondary thickening of the adjacent bursae. Compressive load from hip adduction, such as crossing the legs or lying on the side, combined with tensile overload contributes to the tendon change. As with other tendinopathies the tissue shows disorganised collagen and failed healing rather than a predominantly inflammatory bursitis.
additionalDifferentials: Lumbar radiculopathy or referred spinal pain
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound to assess the gluteal tendons and bursal change and to guide injection
MRI for tendinopathy and tears and to exclude hip joint or bony pathology
Plain radiographs of the hip and pelvis to assess the joint and enthesophytes
Clinical provocative testing (resisted abduction, single-leg stance)
Assessment of the lumbar spine as a source of referred pain
redFlags: Rest or night bone pain with systemic features suggesting infection or malignancy
Inability to weight bear or perform single-leg stance suggesting a significant abductor tear
Neurological signs pointing to lumbar radiculopathy
History suggesting a femoral neck stress fracture in an at-risk athlete
reference.prognosis: Most improve with load management and abductor rehabilitation, although symptoms can be persistent; refractory cases may benefit from shockwave therapy or, rarely, surgery for a confirmed tendon tear.
pitfalls: Labelling the problem 'bursitis' and treating with rest or injection rather than progressive abductor loading
Missing a gluteal tendon tear or hip joint pathology
Overlooking referred pain from the lumbar spine
Repeated corticosteroid injections without accompanying rehabilitation
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
management: Base treatment on load management and a progressive gluteal abductor tendon rehabilitation programme
Advise posture and activity modification to reduce compressive load, avoiding leg-crossing and prolonged lying on the affected side
Use simple analgesia and short-term non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for symptom control
Consider a peritrochanteric corticosteroid injection for short-term relief in refractory pain
Offer extracorporeal shockwave therapy for symptoms persisting despite rehabilitation
Reserve surgery for a confirmed gluteal tendon tear failing conservative care, and assess the lumbar spine as a source of referred pain
